title: How to translate school letters for families on Mac: a teacher's routine for 2026
metaTitle: Translate School Letters for Families on Mac: Teacher Routine
description: Translate school letters for families on your Mac with Google Docs and Apple Translate, plus a weekly routine and checks for errors.
intro: To translate school letters for families on a Mac, copy the letter into Google Docs and choose Tools > Translate document. For one sentence or phrase, select it, Control-click, and choose Translate. Then check every date, amount and name before you send it. Machine translation often gets the details wrong.
tldr: Use Tools > Translate document in Google Docs for a full letter. Your original file stays as it is.
For a sentence or phrase, Control-click the selected text on Mac and choose Translate.
Write the English first, in short sentences with full dates. Clean English translates better.
Have a bilingual colleague check dates, money, deadlines and names before anything goes home.
Check your district's student privacy rules before you paste any student details into a tool.

blocks.text: How many families need a translated letter

Start with the size of the problem. The National Center for Education Statistics counts English learners as 10.6% of public school students in fall 2021. That is 5.3 million students. In fall 2011 the share was 9.4%, or 4.6 million students. The count covers students, not households, so it shows the scale but not how many letters your school sends. Your own class list fills in that part.

The spread between states is wide. In fall 2021 the share ran from 0.8% in West Virginia to 20.2% in Texas. In Texas, a translated letter may come home every week. In West Virginia it may come up much less often. Check your own roster before you assume a letter needs translation, or that it does not.
What teachers reported about parent letters in 2018

A ClassDojo survey from 2018 asked more than 560 randomly selected U.S. teachers about language barriers. Of those teachers, 56% worried that parents of English learners did not have enough English to take part in school communication. Among schools, 55% translate parent correspondence into other languages, and 28% do not translate it at all. The survey is old and comes from one company, so read the numbers as a snapshot, not a national measure.
Where the time goes, and what no study measures

No study I could open measures how many hours teachers spend translating letters. You will not find a clean figure for a budget request. The closest source covers all teaching work. A 2025 RAND survey, as summarized by Education Week, found that more than 80% of teachers work beyond contracted hours. Those teachers average about 10 extra hours per week. The same survey found 53% report burnout. Translation is not the cause of those numbers, but it sits inside them.

You can measure your own cost. Keep a simple log for a few weeks. Write down each letter, the minutes it took to rewrite, translate and check, and whether a colleague had to fix anything. Your log will tell you more than a national average. It also gives you a concrete figure to bring to your principal when you ask for a shared process.
A worked example: one permission slip, start to finish

Say the school sends home a field trip permission slip. It is written in English, has a return date, a fee and a consent box. The family reads Spanish at home. Here is the routine that works on a Mac, from English draft to sent email.

items: Rewrite the English first. Shorten each sentence and write the date in full, with the weekday and month.
Open the slip in Google Docs. If the file is a Word document and Translate document does not appear, convert it to Google Docs first, as Google's help page advises.
Choose Tools > Translate document. Enter a name for the copy, pick Spanish, and click Translate.
Read the Spanish copy in the new window. Check the return date, the fee and the consent line against the English original by hand.
Control-click any sentence that reads oddly, then choose Translate to see a second version. Replace only text you have already checked.
Send the English and Spanish together in one Gmail message, or attach both files. Keep a copy in your records.

blocks.text: The table shows the main options. Apple's Mac Help page covers translating selected text. It does not describe whole files, so use Google Docs for a full letter. Pages does not appear in the sources I checked as having a whole-document translate command, so confirm it yourself before you plan around it.
Translate a passage with Apple Translate on Mac

Select the text in a document, email or message. Control-click it, then choose Translate. Read the translated version in the pop-up. If it is right, choose Replace with Translation to swap the original text for the translation. Apple's page says that option replaces the original, so copy the English somewhere safe first.

Two settings matter. Download languages for offline use in System Settings > General > Language & Region > Translation Languages. Apple says offline translations may be less accurate than server-based ones. On-Device Mode processes translations on your Mac even when you are online. Check your district's rules before you assume that mode meets them.
Translate a whole letter in Google Docs

Google Docs is the better tool for a full letter. Open the document and choose Tools > Translate document. Enter a name for the new copy, pick the language, and click Translate. The translated copy opens in a new window and saves to Google Drive. The original stays intact, so you can compare the two.

Keep the English next to the translation while you check. Many teachers put both versions in one document, side by side in two columns. The steps for columns are in [How to create columns in Google Docs on Mac](/how-to/create-columns-in-google-docs). Read the two columns line by line, not as a whole page.
Where machine translation goes wrong

Machine translation is fast. It also gets details wrong in ways that matter. In Minnesota, staff at South Washington County found Somali and Hmong translations not always as accurate as Spanish. In Rochester, a translation mistranslated the word referendum in ballot-measure messages. These are news reports quoting district staff, not controlled tests. They still show the pattern to watch for.

St. Paul's newsletters carry a note that the translation function 'may be inaccurate or incomplete.' Its principals are told not to send machine translations in emails or robocalls without staff verification. That is a fair standard for a classroom letter too. A second reader turns a quick draft into a letter you can send.
Check the lines that cannot be wrong
Some lines carry most of the risk. Read these against the English, one at a time, before you send.

items: Money, including fees and whether a payment is optional
Names of people, places and the school
Yes or no choices and signature lines

blocks.text: Ask a bilingual colleague or the front office to check those lines. Do it even when the translation looks clean. Clean text can still carry a wrong date.

blocks.title: Student information comes first
blocks.text: Student records are private. Before you paste a student's name, grades or health details into any translation or AI tool, check your district's rules. Some tools keep what you send. Follow your employer's rules on student data, not a habit from last year.
Homework, forms and replies

Homework needs a lighter touch. Most worksheets mix short instructions with problems. Translate the instructions, and keep the problems in their original form unless the student needs the full text. Ask the family which format helps most. Some want the whole sheet. Others want only the directions.

Forms with boxes are harder. A translated form can push text out of its box or shift a signature line. Keep the original layout, then put the translated instructions on a separate page or in the email body. Families can sign the original and read the translation beside it.

Replies are a separate problem. A parent may answer in their own language. Ask a colleague to read it, or select the reply and use Apple Translate on Mac to get the gist. Write your answer in plain English, then send it in both languages if you can. The steps for quick replies are in [How to reply to parent emails quickly on Mac](/for/teachers/problems/reply-parent-emails-quickly-teachers).
Sending the letter in Gmail

Gmail is where many letters leave your desk. Attach the translated copy as a PDF, or paste both languages into one message. Put the English first if your school expects it. Write the subject line in English, and add the family's language where it helps. When Gmail shortcuts are on, ⌘ Return sends the message. If you need a copy on record, see [How to add CC and BCC in Gmail on Mac](/how-to/add-cc-and-bcc-in-gmail).
What research says about family communication

A 2020 meta-analysis in Educational Psychology Review looked at 77 family-school partnership studies, with 438 effect sizes. Its academic achievement effect was δ = 0.25. The authors found that school-to-home communication contributed significantly to intervention effects, along with home-based involvement and collaboration.

Two limits matter here. These studies test family-school programs, not translation alone. The analysis also found that two-way communication worked better for older students. So a letter is one part of a relationship, not the whole of it. The analysis found no significant moderation by race or ethnicity.
Mistakes people make with translated letters

items: Translating a messy English draft. Fix the English first, or the translation copies the mess.
Trusting the first output. Read the translation against the original, line by line.
Replacing text before you check it. Use Replace with Translation only after you read the result.
Forgetting the English original. Keep it on file so you can answer questions from families.
Writing dates in shorthand. Spell out the weekday and month.
Using personal accounts for student records. Check your district's rules first.

blocks.text: Where Lazur fits, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where a menu item sits and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to do something and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click. That helps when you cannot find Tools > Translate document or the Control-click options in a new app.

Lazur does not click buttons, edit files or run other apps for you. It is not a plugin or add-in for any app. It does not replace the bilingual check. Lazur can help you draft a simpler English version first, which is often the best fix. You still read every date and amount yourself.

Dictation is included. Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. The personal dictionary keeps school names spelled right. Snippets can hold a standard closing line for family letters. Clipboard slots hold a checked phrase you reuse.

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Read that policy yourself, and still follow your district's rules on student data.

blocks.text: Pick the letter that goes home most often, such as the weekly newsletter or permission slip. Write an English version that translates cleanly, then save the checked translation in a Drive folder. Reuse it next time, and update both versions together.

faq.question: How do I translate a school letter on a Mac?
faq.answer: For a full letter, copy it into Google Docs and choose Tools > Translate document. For one sentence or phrase, select it, Control-click, and choose Translate. Check dates, money and names against the English before you send.

faq.question: Does Apple Translate work on a whole document?
faq.answer: Apple's Mac Help page describes translating selected text only. It does not describe whole files. For a full letter, use Google Docs. Confirm any whole-document option in an Apple app yourself before you plan around it.

faq.question: Why does Translate document not appear in Google Docs?
faq.answer: Google's help page says the file is likely open in Microsoft Office. Convert it to Google Docs first, then choose Tools > Translate document again.

faq.question: Is machine translation accurate enough for school letters?
faq.answer: Not on its own for names, dates, money and deadlines. Minnesota districts reported accuracy gaps between languages and one mistranslated word in a ballot notice. Have a staff member check high-risk lines before anything goes home.

faq.question: Should I translate all of the homework?
faq.answer: Translate the instructions first. Keep the problems in their original form unless the student needs the full text. Ask the family which format helps them most.

faq.question: Can Lazur translate my letters for me?
faq.answer: Lazur can explain menu items, point at them, guide you through steps, dictate text and draft a simpler English version. It does not replace a bilingual check, and it does not click Translate for you. You still read the result.

faq.question: Do I need to follow rules before I paste student information into a tool?
faq.answer: Yes. Student records are private. Check your district's rules before you paste a student's name, grades or health details into any translation or AI tool.

faq.question: Can I download languages for offline use on a Mac?
faq.answer: Yes. Go to System Settings > General > Language & Region > Translation Languages and download the languages you need. Apple says offline translations may be less accurate than server-based ones.

costs.title: Your evenings
costs.text: No study I could find measures the hours teachers spend translating letters. The closest figure covers all teaching work. More than 80% of teachers work beyond contracted hours, averaging 10 extra hours per week, according to RAND's 2025 survey as reported by Education Week. Translation is one line in that load.

costs.title: Families who miss the message
costs.text: In a 2020 meta-analysis of 77 family-school studies, school-to-home communication contributed significantly to intervention effects. A letter a family cannot read cannot carry that message. The study does not measure translated letters, so treat this as a reason to care, not a measured loss.

costs.title: Wrong dates, money and deadlines
costs.text: A mistranslated word can change the meaning of a notice. Rochester's example of the word referendum in a ballot notice is anecdotal, but it shows the stakes. A missed return date or a wrong fee can cost a family money or a field trip seat.

costs.title: Trust with families
costs.text: In a 2018 ClassDojo survey, 56% of teachers worried that parents of English learners lacked enough English to take part. That is a worry, not a measured drop in participation. A letter that reads badly in translation can still make a family feel like an outsider.

costs.title: Tools that only some staff use
costs.text: At Mounds View, the TalkingPoints app sent more than 23,000 messages to families, mostly in Spanish, Somali and Arabic. Only about 40% of staff use the app, so the work stays uneven. A tool helps less when most colleagues do not use it.

causes.title: Letters start in English by default
causes.text: Many letters begin as English templates, and translation gets added at the end, if at all. A 2018 ClassDojo survey found 28% of schools do not translate parent correspondence. When English is the default, a teacher writing late in the evening may not think about translation until the letter is finished.

causes.title: Nobody owns the translation step
causes.text: A letter often moves from teacher to office to principal. Each person may assume someone else will translate it. Unless your school names an owner for that step, the job drifts to whoever is last in line, and that is often the teacher.

causes.title: Machine translation looks finished
causes.text: A translated paragraph reads smoothly, even when one word is wrong. Smooth text makes people stop checking. Minnesota districts reported lower accuracy for Somali and Hmong than for Spanish, and one mistranslated word in a ballot notice. The risk grows when no one reads the output.

causes.title: Teacher writing is not built for translation
causes.text: Long sentences, idioms, abbreviations and school jargon carry over badly into another language. A phrase such as 'send it in on Friday' or a shortened program name can change meaning. Plain sentences with one idea each give a translation tool less to get wrong.

causes.title: The tools split documents from phrases
causes.text: Apple's Mac Help page describes translating selected text, not whole files. Google Docs translates whole documents, but only for files that are already Google Docs. Teachers often copy paragraphs one at a time, which can lose layout and line order.

causes.title: The workload leaves no spare hours
causes.text: RAND's 2025 survey, as summarized by Education Week, found that more than 80% of teachers work beyond contracted hours. Under that load, a translation task gets pushed to the weekend. The survey does not measure translation, but it explains why small extra tasks pile up.

fixes.title: Write the English so it translates
fixes.text: Keep each sentence to one idea. Write dates in full, with the weekday and month. Replace idioms and school shorthand with plain words. Clean English gives any translation tool less to get wrong, and it costs nothing to try.

fixes.title: Translate whole letters in Google Docs
fixes.text: Open the letter in Google Docs and choose Tools > Translate document. Name the copy, pick the language, and click Translate. The original stays intact. If the option is missing, convert the Word file to Google Docs first.

fixes.title: Use Apple Translate for one phrase at a time
fixes.text: Select the text, Control-click it, and choose Translate. Use Replace with Translation only after you check the result, and copy the English first. For offline use, download languages in System Settings > General > Language & Region > Translation Languages.

fixes.title: Keep a folder of checked translations
fixes.text: Save each checked translation in a Google Drive folder, labeled by language, letter type and date. Reuse the permission slip and newsletter versions. Update the English and the translation together, so they never drift apart.

fixes.title: Put a second reader on the risky lines
fixes.text: Ask a bilingual colleague, a family liaison or the front office to check dates, money, deadlines, names and signature lines. Give them the English next to the translation. A fast read on the risky lines beats a slow read on the whole letter.

fixes.title: Lay out English and translation side by side
fixes.text: Put both versions in two columns in one Google Doc, or in two sections of one email. Side-by-side layout makes mismatches easier to spot. The column steps are in How to create columns in Google Docs on Mac.

fixes.title: Ask families which language and format they want
fixes.text: Add a short line to a sign-up form that asks for the preferred language and whether the family wants the full letter or only the key points. Keep the answers in your school's approved system, and ask again each year.

plan.label: Monday
plan.title: Sort the letters
plan.text: List every letter, permission slip and homework sheet going home this week. Mark the families who need another language. Use the home language list your school keeps, and follow its rules on who can see it.

plan.label: Tuesday
plan.title: Write the English first
plan.text: Shorten each sentence. Write dates in full. Cut idioms and abbreviations. If you want a second pass, ask Lazur to draft a plainer version, then read it yourself before you translate.

plan.label: Wednesday
plan.title: Translate and save
plan.text: Run whole letters through Tools > Translate document in Google Docs. Use Control-click for a single phrase. Save each checked version in one Drive folder, labeled by language and date.

plan.label: Thursday
plan.title: Check the risky lines
plan.text: Read dates, money, deadlines, names and signature lines against the English. Send those lines to a bilingual colleague or the front office and ask for a quick read.

plan.label: Friday
plan.title: Send and log
plan.text: Send through Gmail with the English and the translation together. Log who received it and in which language. Set a reminder to follow up with families who have not replied.
